title: Pain, fear and the clench
hookLine: pain is sensation and emotion; fear and bracing can feed it, and loosening the grip helps some people
carry: fear and bracing are part of the hurt

lines: A STUBBED TOE ON A GOOD DAY.
THE SAME TOE ON A BAD ONE.
cards: A stubbed toe at the end of a great day: a yelp, a laugh, forgotten in a minute. The same stubbed toe at the end of a terrible day: it's the last straw, and it throbs for an hour. Same toe.

Same doorframe. Something besides the toe is deciding how much it hurts. After days of scripture, novels and memoirs, this path turns to the lab and the clinic, which have their own careful things to say.

teach.b: First, what pain is. The International Association for the Study of Pain, a body of pain researchers and clinicians, defines pain as an unpleasant sensory and emotional experience. Both words matter.
Pain is real in the body, and it's also shaped by what's going on in the mind. That doesn't mean it's imagined. It means it's whole-person.

Pain researchers describe a loop, sometimes called the fear-avoidance model: a person in pain fears it, braces against it, moves less, watches for it, and for some people that loop keeps the pain going and makes it worse.
Tensing around an ache can feed it. Third, attention. The psychologist William James wrote: "My experience is what I agree to attend to."
Pain grabs attention, and attention can feed pain.

teach.h: NOT A CURE. A SOFTER GRIP.
teach.b: But attention can also be placed differently: not away from the pain, not clenched around it, but softer and wider. Fourth, what mindfulness courses can and can't do.

Programs such as Jon Kabat-Zinn's mindfulness-based stress reduction, which he says draws on Buddhist meditation, teach people with long-term pain to notice the sensation itself, without the bracing and the story.

In some studies, people in these courses report that their pain bothers them less, and some report less pain. Not everyone. It isn't a cure, and the science never says the pain was all in someone's head.
It says something smaller and useful: the fear and the clench around an ache are part of the hurt, and for some people, those parts can soften.

how: Some pain clinics and hospitals offer mindfulness-based courses, and pain psychologists help people notice and loosen the fear and bracing around long-term pain, alongside medical care.

o: pressing hard on a sore spot to numb it
pretending a pain isn't there until it fades
loosening the fear and bracing around an ache

games.q: inside the science of pain — tap the pairs.

s: if the mind shapes pain, the pain is imagined
the definition says sensory and emotional: real in the body, and whole-person.
fear and bracing can keep pain going for some people
the fear-avoidance model describes that loop.
in some studies some people report less pain or less bother; not everyone, and not a cure.

games.q: your back aches after a long day. what does the fear-avoidance research suggest can make it worse?
o: bracing, watching for it, and moving as little as possible.
games.why: the loop of fearing, bracing and avoiding can keep pain going for some people. loosening the grip is today's practice.

practice: Find one mild ache, a stiff neck, a tired back, a sore foot; if an ache is new or severe, that's for a doctor, not a sit.
Let your attention rest near it and notice what's around it, muscles bracing, breath held, a face tensed, and on each out-breath let one of those soften a little.
You're not making the ache go away, just loosening the grip around it.

wordCard.voice: Soften around it. Pain is sensation and emotion; fear and bracing can feed it, and loosening the grip helps some people. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali (also Sanskrit), written in Devanagari: feeling, the pleasant, painful or neutral tone of an experience, which Buddhist meditation teaches people to notice.

carryVoice: Your line: fear and bracing are part of the hurt. The ache may stay; for some, the clench around it eases. See you tomorrow.
